Painted Venus arriving by shell and springtime itself. Savonarola talked him into burning some of his own nudes, which art history has never forgiven.
Venice's master of flesh tones so particular that 'titian' became a hair colour. Kings waited; the paint could not be rushed.
Painted abundance with such conviction that 'Rubenesque' entered the language. Also a working diplomat — the curves funded the treaties.
Court painter who ended up painting nightmares on his own dining-room walls. In between, one very famous undressed maja and an inquisition summons for it.
Scandalised Paris twice in two years with nudes who made eye contact. The critics fainted; modern art got up.
Painted women in rivers of gold leaf and kept cats and no explanations. Vienna blushed and commissioned more.
Drew the human body as all elbows, knuckles and truth. A century later the poses still look uncomfortable, which was the point.
Sculpted flesh so alive he was accused of casting from live bodies. The Kiss and The Thinker answered the accusation permanently.
The Athenian who first dared a full-scale female nude in marble. Antiquity never emotionally recovered.
Sculpted his ideal woman, fell in love with the marble, and Aphrodite — amused — made her real. The original parasocial relationship.
Threw away the corset and the shoes and invented modern dance in bare feet and loose silk. Scandalous then, syllabus now.
Conquered Paris in a skirt of sixteen bananas, then spied for the French Resistance and marched on Washington. The bananas were the least of her.
The striptease intellectual — quoted philosophy while removing gloves, wrote a bestselling memoir, and made the tease smarter than the reveal.
Two ostrich fans, impeccable choreography, and technically no nudity anyone could prove. Arrested four times in one day at the 1933 World's Fair and acquitted with applause.
The Queen of Pinups — the bangs launched a hairstyle that has never once retired.
Manet's nude who stares straight back. Paris rioted; guards were posted; the gaze won.
A nude woman picnicking with two fully dressed men, all very calm about it. The Salon refused it; the refusal made it immortal.
Goya's reclining maja, painted with a clothed twin so the owner could swap them when company called. The Inquisition asked questions anyway.
Ingres' languid nude with three vertebrae too many. Critics counted; the extra spine stayed; elegance beat anatomy.
Titian's Venus, entirely unbothered, with a small dog asleep at her feet. Mark Twain called it the foulest painting in the world, which is a five-star review from Twain.
Klimt's Danaë receiving Zeus as a shower of gold, which is mythology's most expensive euphemism.
Ingres finished this circular crowd of bathers at 82, proving some artistic interests never retire.
Duchamp's nude as a motion blur. 1913 America called it 'an explosion in a shingle factory' and queued around the block to be offended.
Courbet's most direct painting, hidden behind curtains and green screens by a century of owners. The Musée d'Orsay finally just hung it, and posted a guard.
Velázquez's Venus at her mirror — slashed seven times by a suffragette in 1914, restored, and hanging serenely ever since. The mirror reflects impossibly; painters call it artistic licence.
Picasso's five nudes with mask faces that broke painting in half. Even his friends hated it for a decade; the twentieth century apologised eventually.
Modigliani's reclining nude sold for $170 million — his 1917 exhibition of them was shut by police on opening day. The market recovered.
Delacroix's Liberty storming the barricade, flag up, dress down to the waist. France put her on money and stamps, chest and all.
Bosch's triptych of several hundred nudes doing unexplainable things with giant fruit and musical instruments. Five centuries of scholars, zero consensus.

Michelangelo filled the Sistine's altar wall with nudes; the Church later hired a painter to add loincloths. He is remembered forever as Il Braghettone — 'the breeches-maker'. A warning to all editors.
The discus thrower, wound like a spring, wearing regulation ancient athletic kit: nothing.
Hercules leaning exhausted on his club, muscles on muscles. Gym culture's founding document.
For three centuries the official most beautiful object in the world, per every Grand Tour guidebook. Fashions changed; the abs did not.
A priest and his sons losing a wrestling match with sea serpents, nude and magnificent about it. Michelangelo watched it dug out of a vineyard in 1506.
A defeated warrior, nude with his torc, dying with more dignity than most statues manage standing up.
A 55-metre chalk man on an English hillside, carrying a club and an erection visible from aircraft. The National Trust re-chalks him faithfully, all of him.
Eleven centimetres of limestone curves, thirty thousand years old. The first known artwork of a human is a nude, which settled the genre question early.
Carved from mammoth ivory at least 40,000 years ago — the oldest depiction of a human being found so far. Also nude. It has always been like this.

Praxiteles' original — the first life-size female nude, so famous that Knidos built a shrine with a door on both sides. One admirer's overnight visit left a stain the guides pointed out for centuries.
Brussels' 1987 answer to its famous boy: a little girl, squatting, equally unbothered. Protected by an iron grille from admirers and equal-opportunity vandals.
The third member of Brussels' urinating-statue family: a mutt at a bollard. The city committed to the bit completely.
Copenhagen's bronze mermaid, topless, patient, and beheaded twice by vandals with grudges nobody understands. She was recast; she always is.
A classical pillar: a god's head on top, genitals halfway down, nothing else. Athens had hundreds; the night someone vandalised them all became an actual state emergency in 415 BC.
